entities.summary:
The Freedom Party of Austria (Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs, FPÖ), founded in 1956 from former Nazis and pan-German nationalists, is Europe's most enduring far-right populist party — pioneering the anti-immigration, nationalist, anti-EU rhetoric that defined European populist right-wing politics from the 1990s onward. Jörg Haider's leadership (1986-2000) transformed the FPÖ from a minor party to a major force receiving 27% of the vote in 1999, triggering EU sanctions against Austria — the first time the EU imposed diplomatic measures against a member state for a party's electoral success.

The FPÖ was founded in 1956 to incorporate former Nazis and members of the Greater German People's Party into Austrian democracy through a pro-Western, liberal nationalist party. Under Anton Reinthaller and then Norbert Steger, the FPÖ was a small liberal party. Jörg Haider's takeover in 1986 transformed it with anti-immigration rhetoric, Waldheim-era historical revisionism, and charismatic populism.

Haider's 27% result in 1999, and the FPÖ's entry into coalition government with the ÖVP in 2000, triggered EU diplomatic sanctions (the 'Fourteen Against One' isolation of Austria) that were the first such EU action against a member government. This controversy established the FPÖ as the model that Marine Le Pen, Viktor Orbán, Nigel Farage, and Donald Trump studied and adapted. The 2019 Ibiza Scandal — hidden cameras recording FPÖ leader Heinz-Christian Strache apparently offering government contracts to a fake Russian oligarch's niece — brought down the coalition and demonstrated the corruption risks of populist government.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Austria's FPÖ was Europe's first major populist far-right party to enter government — triggering the EU's first diplomatic sanctions against a member state and becoming the template that Marine Le Pen, Viktor Orbán, and Donald Trump studied to transform their own movements.
